title: Atomic Structure and Periodicity
description: Light, quantization and the quantum mechanical atom, and how electron configurations explain the periodic table.
overview: The nuclear model leaves a puzzle. A negative electron orbiting a positive nucleus should radiate energy and spiral inward in a fraction of a nanosecond, yet atoms are stable and emit light only at sharp, characteristic wavelengths. Resolving this took quantum mechanics, in which energy is exchanged in discrete amounts and electrons behave like waves.

This chapter builds the modern picture of the atom from the properties of light, through the Bohr model to orbitals and quantum numbers, and then uses electron configurations to explain the periodic trends that organize chemistry.
objectives: Relate the wavelength, frequency and energy of light, and calculate photon energies.
Explain the photoelectric effect and the de Broglie relation.
Use the Bohr model and the Rydberg equation to predict hydrogen spectral lines.
Assign the four quantum numbers and describe s, p and d orbitals.
Write electron configurations for atoms and ions using the Aufbau principle, the Pauli exclusion principle and Hund’s rule.
Explain trends in atomic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity.

sections.title: Light and the electromagnetic spectrum
body: Light is **electromagnetic radiation**: oscillating electric and magnetic fields traveling through vacuum at c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. A wave is described by its **wavelength** λ, the distance between crests, and its **frequency** ν, the number of crests passing a point per second (hertz, s⁻¹). They are tied together by
The electromagnetic spectrum runs from radio waves (long wavelength, low frequency) through microwaves, infrared, visible light (about 400 nm violet to 700 nm red), ultraviolet, X-rays and γ rays.
Light also comes in packets. A **photon** of frequency ν carries energy
where h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is **Planck’s constant**. Short wavelengths mean high-energy photons, which is why ultraviolet light damages skin and visible light does not.

example.title: Energy of a photon
example.problem: Find the energy of a photon of green light, λ = 500 nm, and the energy per mole of such photons.
solution: This is comparable to the energy of a chemical bond, which is why visible and ultraviolet light can drive reactions.

check.q: Which has the higher energy per photon?

sections.title: Quantization and wave–particle duality
body: Classical physics predicted that a hot object should emit infinite energy at short wavelengths. In 1900 Max Planck resolved this by assuming that matter can emit or absorb energy only in discrete amounts, E = hν. Energy is **quantized**.

When light strikes a metal, electrons are ejected only if the frequency exceeds a threshold, no matter how intense the light. Above the threshold, the number of electrons scales with intensity, and their kinetic energy scales with frequency. Classical wave theory cannot explain this. Einstein (1905) proposed that light consists of photons, and that each photon gives all its energy to a single electron. The photon must pay the **work function** Φ, the minimum energy to free an electron from the metal, and the remainder becomes kinetic energy:

example.title: Photoelectric effect in sodium
example.problem: The work function of sodium is 3.65 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (2.28 eV). (a) What is the longest wavelength that ejects electrons? (b) What is the kinetic energy of electrons ejected by 300 nm light?

body: If light, a wave, has particle character, perhaps matter has wave character. In 1924 Louis de Broglie proposed that a particle of mass m and speed v has wavelength

Electron diffraction by crystals confirmed this in 1927. A baseball (0.145 kg at 40 m s⁻¹) has λ ≈ 10⁻³⁴ m, far too small to observe. An electron at 1.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ has λ = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ / (9.109 × 10⁻³¹ × 1.0 × 10⁶) = 0.73 nm, comparable to atomic dimensions, so wave behavior dominates. This **wave–particle duality** underlies electron microscopy and the quantum description of atoms.

wrong: Ejects electrons with more kinetic energy

check.q: Why do we not observe the wave nature of a thrown baseball?
check.a: Its de Broglie wavelength is far too small
wrong: Its speed is too low for a wavelength to exist

sections.title: The Bohr model and atomic spectra
body: A heated gas emits light only at discrete wavelengths, a **line spectrum**. Hydrogen’s visible lines (656, 486, 434, 410 nm) obey a simple formula found by Balmer and generalized by Rydberg:
Here n₁ and n₂ are integers with n₂ > n₁. In 1913 Bohr explained this with a model: the electron in hydrogen can occupy only certain circular orbits, with energies

The lowest level, n = 1, is the **ground state**. The electron does not radiate in an orbit. It emits a photon only when it drops to a lower level, with hν equal to the energy difference, and absorbs one when it rises. Lines ending on n = 1 are ultraviolet (the Lyman series). Those ending on n = 2 are in the visible (the **Balmer series**), and those ending on n = 3 are in the infrared (Paschen).

body: The Bohr model works only for one-electron species (H, He⁺, Li²⁺), and it wrongly treats the electron as moving on a fixed path. Its lasting contribution is the idea that atoms have discrete energy levels, which the quantum mechanical model keeps.

Which hydrogen series lies in the ultraviolet?

subs.title: Uncertainty and the wave function
body: Heisenberg’s **uncertainty principle** states that position and momentum cannot both be known exactly:

An electron confined to an atom therefore cannot follow a definite path. Instead, Schrödinger’s equation gives a **wave function** ψ for each allowed state. By Born’s interpretation, ψ² at a point is the **probability density** of finding the electron there. A region where the electron is likely to be found is an **orbital**. Solving the equation for hydrogen gives exactly the Bohr energies, with no assumptions about orbits.

subs.title: Quantum numbers and orbital shapes
body: Each orbital is labeled by three quantum numbers, and an electron in it by a fourth:

head: Symbol
Name
Allowed values
Determines
rows: Shape; defines the **subshell** (s, p, d, f for l = 0, 1, 2, 3)

body: A shell n contains n subshells and n² orbitals, and holds up to 2n² electrons. A subshell holds 2(2l + 1) electrons: 2 for s, 6 for p, 10 for d and 14 for f. The 2p subshell, for example, has n = 2 and l = 1, with three orbitals (m_{l} = −1, 0, +1).

list: **p orbitals** (l = 1) have two lobes along an axis (p_{x}, p_{y}, p_{z}) with a **node**, a plane of zero probability, at the nucleus.
**d orbitals** (l = 2) mostly have four lobes, five orbitals in all.
An orbital has n − 1 total nodes: l angular nodes and n − l − 1 radial nodes. A 3s orbital has two radial nodes.

body.note: In hydrogen all subshells of the same n have the same energy. In atoms with several electrons, repulsion splits them, and the order within a shell is s < p < d < f.

check.q: Which set of quantum numbers is NOT allowed?
check.why: l must be less than n, so l = 2 is not allowed when n = 2.

check.q: How many orbitals are in the n = 3 shell?
How many radial nodes does a 3p orbital have?

sections.title: Electron configurations
body: The **electron configuration** of an atom lists the occupied subshells and the number of electrons in each, for example 1s²2s²2p⁶. Three rules produce the ground-state configuration:

list: **Aufbau principle:** fill orbitals from lowest energy upward. The order follows the Madelung (n + l) rule: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p. Subshells with a lower n + l fill first, and for ties the lower n fills first.
**Pauli exclusion principle:** no two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins.
**Hund’s rule:** electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly, with parallel spins, before pairing. This minimizes electron–electron repulsion.

body: Noble-gas shorthand replaces the core: sulfur is [Ne]3s²3p⁴ and iron is [Ar]3d⁶4s². The outer-shell electrons that take part in bonding are the **valence electrons**. For a main-group element they equal the group number (units digit): sulfur has six. The inner **core electrons** do not usually participate.

Half-filled and filled d subshells are unusually stable, so chromium is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ (not 3d⁴4s²) and copper is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹. When a transition metal forms a cation, the ns electrons leave before the (n − 1)d electrons, because once d electrons are present they lie lower in energy. Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶ and Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵.
Species with the same number of electrons are **isoelectronic**: N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Ne, Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and Al³⁺ all have 1s²2s²2p⁶.
A species with unpaired electrons is **paramagnetic** and is drawn into a magnetic field. One with all electrons paired is **diamagnetic** and is weakly repelled.

example.title: Configuration and magnetism
example.problem: Write the ground-state configurations of Mn and Mn²⁺, and state how many unpaired electrons each has.
solution: Mn (Z = 25): [Ar]3d⁵4s². The five 3d electrons occupy five orbitals singly, giving five unpaired electrons.
Mn²⁺ loses the 4s electrons first: [Ar]3d⁵, still with five unpaired electrons. Both are paramagnetic.

check.q: What is the electron configuration of Fe³⁺?
How many unpaired electrons does a nitrogen atom have?
check.why: Nitrogen is 1s²2s²2p³. By Hund’s rule the three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals.
Zn is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s², with all electrons paired.

subs.title: Effective nuclear charge and atomic size
body: An outer electron feels the nucleus’s charge +Z attenuated by the inner electrons that **shield** it. The net attraction is the **effective nuclear charge**, Z_{eff} = Z − S, where S is the shielding. Across a period, Z rises by one for each element while the added electron goes into the same shell and shields poorly, so Z_{eff} increases. Down a group, new shells are added, so the outer electrons are farther away and well shielded.

This gives the trend in **atomic radius**: it decreases from left to right across a period and increases down a group. A cation is smaller than its parent atom (fewer electrons, less repulsion, often a lost shell), and an anion is larger. In an isoelectronic series, the radius falls as the nuclear charge increases: O²⁻ (140 pm) > F⁻ (133 pm) > Na⁺ (102 pm) > Mg²⁺ (72 pm) > Al³⁺ (54 pm).

subs.title: Ionization energy and electron affinity
body: The **first ionization energy**, IE₁, is the energy to remove one electron from a gaseous atom: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻. It increases across a period (rising Z_{eff}, shrinking radius) and decreases down a group. Two dips interrupt the trend in each period: IE₁ of B is lower than Be, because the 2p electron is higher in energy than a 2s electron, and IE₁ of O is lower than N, because the paired 2p electron is repelled by its partner.

body: **Successive ionization energies** reveal the electron shells. For Mg (IE₁ 738, IE₂ 1451, IE₃ 7733 kJ mol⁻¹), the large jump after the second electron shows that Mg has two valence electrons and that the third comes from the 2p core.

The **electron affinity** is the energy released when a gaseous atom gains an electron (more negative values mean stronger attraction). Halogens have the most negative values: Cl, −349 kJ mol⁻¹. Noble gases and Group 2 elements have values near zero or positive, because the added electron must enter a new subshell or shell.

subs.title: Electronegativity and the periodic law
body: **Electronegativity** is the tendency of an atom in a bond to attract the shared electrons. On Pauling’s scale it runs from 0.7 (Cs) to 3.98 (F), and increases across a period and up a group, as ionization energy does. Typical values: F 3.98, O 3.44, N 3.04, Cl 3.16, C 2.55, H 2.20, Na 0.93.

Mendeleev arranged the elements by atomic mass in 1869 and left gaps for undiscovered elements, predicting the properties of “eka-silicon,” which Winkler found in 1886 as germanium. Moseley’s 1913 X-ray measurements showed that the true ordering variable is atomic number, which fixed the few places where mass order fails (Ar and K, Te and I). The **periodic law**: properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic number.

check.why: All are isoelectronic (18 electrons); the one with the fewest protons is largest.

Why is the first ionization energy of oxygen lower than that of nitrogen?
check.a: A paired 2p electron in oxygen is repelled by its partner
wrong: Oxygen has a larger atomic radius
Oxygen has a lower nuclear charge

quiz.q: What is the energy of one photon of ultraviolet light with wavelength 250 nm?
quiz.why: E = hc/λ = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴)(2.998 × 10⁸)/(2.50 × 10⁻⁷ m) = 7.95 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Leaving the wavelength in nanometers gives 7.95 × 10⁻²⁸, and h/λ omits c.

quiz.q: Beam A has wavelength 400 nm and beam B has wavelength 800 nm. Per photon, beam A carries
wrong: four times the energy of B
the same energy as B if the beams have equal intensity
quiz.why: Photon energy is E = hc/λ, so it is inversely proportional to wavelength. Halving the wavelength doubles the energy of each photon.

quiz.q: A metal has a work function of 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What happens when 600 nm light shines on it?
quiz.a: No electrons are ejected, because each photon carries only 3.31 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
wrong: Electrons are ejected with kinetic energy 8.3 × 10⁻²⁰ J
Electrons are ejected only if the beam is intense enough
Electrons are ejected, since 600 nm is visible light
quiz.why: Each photon gives all its energy to one electron, and 3.31 × 10⁻¹⁹ J is less than Φ. Brighter light means more photons, but none of them has enough energy.

quiz.q: An electron moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s. Its de Broglie wavelength is closest to (m = 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
quiz.why: λ = h/(mv) = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ / (9.109 × 10⁻³¹ × 2.0 × 10⁶) = 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Wavelength is inversely proportional to speed, so doubling v halves λ.

quiz.q: A hydrogen electron falls from n = 3 to n = 1. What is the energy of the emitted photon?
quiz.why: ΔE = 2.178 × 10⁻¹⁸ (1/1² − 1/3²) = 2.178 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 8/9 = 1.94 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. The value 1.45 comes from forgetting to square n, and 1.63 is the n = 2 → 1 transition.

quiz.q: Using the Rydberg equation, the n = 4 → n = 3 line of hydrogen has a wavelength of about
quiz.why: 1/λ = 1.097 × 10⁷ (1/9 − 1/16) = 5.33 × 10⁵ m⁻¹, so λ = 1.88 × 10⁻⁶ m. Lines ending on n = 3 are the Paschen series. The other wavelengths belong to 3 → 2, 4 → 2 and 2 → 1.

quiz.q: Which statement follows from the Heisenberg uncertainty principle?
quiz.a: The more precisely an electron's position is known, the less precisely its momentum can be known
wrong: Better instruments can make Δx · Δp equal to zero
An electron in an s orbital has an exactly known momentum
An electron follows a definite path, but we cannot measure it
quiz.why: Δx · Δp ≥ ħ/2 is a limit built into nature, not a measurement error. It is why electrons in atoms are described by orbitals instead of paths.

quiz.q: How many electrons can the 4f subshell hold?
quiz.why: For f, l = 3, so there are 2l + 1 = 7 orbitals with two electrons each. The number 7 counts orbitals, not electrons.

quiz.q: What is the total number of nodes in a 4d orbital?
quiz.why: An orbital has n − 1 nodes in all. For 4d these are l = 2 angular nodes and n − l − 1 = 1 radial node.

quiz.q: How many subshells are there in the n = 4 shell?
wrong: 3, since l can only reach n − 1 = 3
quiz.why: l runs from 0 to n − 1, giving n subshells: l = 0, 1, 2, 3. The number 16 is n², the count of orbitals.

quiz.q: How many unpaired electrons does the Co²⁺ ion (Z = 27) have?
quiz.why: Co is [Ar]3d⁷4s². The 4s electrons are removed first, leaving [Ar]3d⁷, in which five orbitals hold seven electrons: two pairs and three unpaired.

quiz.q: Why is the ground state of copper [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ rather than the Aufbau-predicted [Ar]3d⁹4s²?
quiz.a: A completely filled 3d subshell is especially stable
wrong: The 4s subshell can hold only one electron in copper
A single electron in 4s lowers repulsion between the 3d electrons
Electrons always fill d subshells before s subshells
quiz.why: Filled and half-filled d subshells are unusually stable, so one 4s electron moves to 3d. Copper and chromium are the standard exceptions.

quiz.q: A student writes the ground state of carbon as 1s²2s²2p_x²2p_y¹. Which rule does this violate?
quiz.a: Hund's rule: the two 2p electrons should be in separate orbitals with parallel spins
wrong: The Pauli exclusion principle: an orbital can hold only one electron
The Aufbau principle: 2p must fill before 2s
Hund's rule: the 2p electrons should have opposite spins
quiz.why: Degenerate orbitals are filled singly with parallel spins before any pairing, so the correct state is 2p_x¹2p_y¹. Pairing two electrons in one orbital is allowed by Pauli but costs repulsion energy.

quiz.q: Why does atomic radius decrease from sodium to chlorine?
quiz.a: The nuclear charge rises while the added electrons enter the same shell and shield poorly, so Z_eff increases
wrong: The added electrons enter inner shells and shield the valence electrons more
Chlorine has fewer electron shells than sodium
Greater electron repulsion squeezes the valence electrons inward
quiz.why: Across a period each element adds one proton and one electron in the same shell. Electrons in a shell shield one another only weakly, so the outer electrons feel a stronger pull.

quiz.q: Which pair of radius comparisons is correct?
quiz.a: K⁺ is smaller than K, and Br⁻ is larger than Br
wrong: K⁺ is larger than K, and Br⁻ is smaller than Br
K⁺ is smaller than K, and Br⁻ is smaller than Br
K⁺ is larger than K, and Br⁻ is larger than Br
quiz.why: A cation has fewer electrons, less repulsion and often one fewer shell, so it is smaller than its atom. An anion has extra repulsion and a larger radius.

quiz.q: An element has successive ionization energies (kJ/mol) of 578, 1817, 2745, 11577 and 14842. How many valence electrons does it have?
quiz.why: The large jump comes after the third electron is removed, showing that the fourth must come from an inner shell. This pattern fits aluminum.

quiz.q: Which list gives the elements Na, H, Cl and C in order of increasing electronegativity?
quiz.why: Pauling values are Na 0.93, H 2.20, C 2.55 and Cl 3.16. Electronegativity increases toward the upper right of the periodic table.

quiz.q: What was the main result of Moseley's X-ray work?
quiz.a: It showed that elements should be ordered by atomic number, not atomic mass
wrong: It confirmed Mendeleev's prediction of eka-silicon, germanium
It showed that elements should be ordered by increasing atomic mass
It showed that the nucleus is made of protons and neutrons
quiz.why: Ordering by atomic number fixes the pairs (Ar and K, Te and I) where mass order puts elements in the wrong column. Winkler, not Moseley, found germanium.

summary: c = λν and E = hν. Light is absorbed and emitted as photons.
The photoelectric effect (KE = hν − Φ) shows light is particulate. Electrons are waves too: λ = h/mv.
Bohr energies E_{n} = −2.178 × 10⁻¹⁸ J/n² explain hydrogen’s spectrum, but only for one-electron species.
Orbitals are described by n, l, m_{l} and m_{s}. A shell holds 2n² electrons.
Configurations follow the Aufbau principle, the Pauli exclusion principle and Hund’s rule. Cations lose ns electrons before (n − 1)d.
Z_{eff} explains the trends: radius falls, and ionization energy and electronegativity rise, across a period. The reverse holds down a group.

problems.q: A laser emits photons of wavelength 632.8 nm. Find the frequency, the energy per photon, and the number of photons emitted per second by a 1.00 mW laser.
Which transition in the hydrogen atom emits light of longer wavelength: n = 4 → 2 or n = 3 → 2? Calculate both wavelengths.
problems.a: n = 3 → 2 is longer (656 nm vs 486 nm).

problems.q: Write the ground-state electron configurations of Cr, Cu²⁺ and Se²⁻. Give the number of unpaired electrons in each.
problems.solution: Cr: [Ar]3d⁵4s¹, 6 unpaired. Cu²⁺: Cu is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹, lose 4s¹ and one 3d: [Ar]3d⁹, 1 unpaired. Se²⁻: Se is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s²4p⁴, add two: [Ar]3d¹⁰4s²4p⁶ = [Kr], 0 unpaired.

problems.q: Rank by increasing first ionization energy: Na, Mg, Al, Si. Explain the irregularity.
problems.solution: Values: Na 496, Al 578, Mg 738, Si 786 kJ mol⁻¹. Al is lower than Mg because the 3p electron it loses is higher in energy and better shielded than Mg’s 3s electron.
